title: Number of Islands
statement: The grid contains 1 (land) and 0 (water). An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically (not diagonally). Return the number of islands.

large_tests.gen_code:
import random
def gen():
    r = random.Random(60)
    return [[[1 if r.random() < 0.7 else 0 for _ in range(300)] for _ in range(300)]]

hints.1_question: Every land cell belongs to exactly one island. How can you make sure you count each island once?
hints.2_nudge: Scan the grid. When you meet unvisited land, count an island and flood-fill (DFS/BFS) all connected land so it is never counted again.
hints.3_big_hint: For each unvisited 1: n += 1; explore with a stack/queue in 4 directions marking cells visited.

known_bugs.name: treats diagonal neighbours as connected
known_bugs.followup: The statement says connected horizontally or vertically. Which neighbours do you visit?

known_bugs.name: counts land cells instead of islands
known_bugs.code:
def numIslands(grid):
    return sum(sum(row) for row in grid)
known_bugs.followup: Does each land cell form its own island, or do connected cells share one?

known_bugs.name: recursive DFS (recursion limit on big islands)
known_bugs.followup: How deep can this recursion get on a 300 x 300 grid that is mostly land, and what is Python's default limit?

followups: How would union-find solve it, and when is that better (dynamic additions)?
Why mark cells visited when pushing, not when popping?
